content.title: Objections to substitution
content.summary: Seven objections to Christ's death in our place, each stated at full strength and answered from Scripture.

answer.text: Christ's death in the place of sinners is not a fringe idea. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 confesses his “substitutionary death” (article II), and Southern Baptists, Calvinist and non-Calvinist, hold it. It has also drawn sharp objections for four centuries. Each objection below is put as strongly as its holders put it, in our own words, and answered first from Scripture.

heldBy: Faustus Socinus (De Jesu Christo Servatore, printed 1594)
Immanuel Kant (Religion within the Boundary of Pure Reason, 1793)
objections.objection: Guilt is the most personal thing a person has. A friend may pay my money debt, because the creditor wants only the sum; a crime belongs to the one who did it. Socinus argued that punishment is personal by nature, and that a law which punishes someone other than the offender has been changed, not satisfied. Kant made it a principle of moral reason: the debt of sin can be discharged only by the guilty, never by an innocent person, however willing he is.

reply.text: Scripture does not teach that Christ's character changed places with ours. Spurgeon, preaching on 2 Corinthians 5:21, insisted that Christ was never guilty in any sense, since guilt cannot belong to someone who had no part in the deed. What Christ bore was the treatment sin deserves: God dealt with him as if he were sin, so that we, united to him, are dealt with as righteous. Israel knew the pattern: on the Day of Atonement the high priest laid the people's iniquities on the goat that carried them away (Leviticus 16:21-22), and the Servant of Isaiah bears the iniquity of many (Isaiah 53:6, 11-12). Boyce draws the same line: Christ was a substitute officially, not personally, treated as a sinner without being one, and God may justly appoint such a representative, as with Adam and the sacrifices. The objection pictures a stranger punished against his will. The gospel speaks of the Judge's own Son taking the place by his own choice (John 10:17-18).

citations.locator: Translator's notes, pp. 257-259 (on Socinus, De Jesu Christo Servatore III.8)

heldBy: Steve Chalke and Alan Mann (The Lost Message of Jesus, 2003)
Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker (feminist theologians, 1989)
objections.objection: A father who plans the suffering and death of his own son is no picture of love; anywhere else we would call it abuse. Chalke and Mann, writing as evangelicals, argued that a God who punishes his Son for what others did contradicts Jesus' own teaching that God is love and that evil is not to be repaid with evil. Some feminist theologians went further: a story in which an innocent child submits to a father's violence, and is praised for it, teaches victims to accept their abuse.

reply.text: The picture works only if the Father and the Son are two beings with opposed wills, one powerful and one helpless. The New Testament says the reverse. The Son is not a child under compulsion but the eternal Son, who gives up his life of his own accord and has the right to take it back (John 10:17-18). The Father gives the Son because he loves the world (John 3:16), and God himself was at work in Christ to reconcile the world (2 Corinthians 5:18-19). Spurgeon, preaching on Isaiah 53:10, called it a slander on the Father to think the cross made him loving: Christ died because God already loved; the Son who suffers is one in being with the Father. R. W. Dale made the same point against a critic of his own day: at the cross the Judge does not inflict suffering on a third party; God, in Christ, chooses to bear it. Nor does the cross tell victims to accept wrong. Jesus' killers acted lawlessly, and God raised him, reversing their verdict (Acts 2:23-24).

citations.locator: No. 1910, 'The Heart of the Gospel' (18 July 1886)

heldBy: The Racovian Catechism of the Polish Brethren (1605)
objections.objection: A debt is either paid or forgiven; it cannot be both. Scripture says God forgives freely. If Christ paid in full, God forgave nothing, and we owe our thanks to Christ rather than to the Father, who merely collected what he was owed. The Racovian Catechism added that a payment made in advance for every future sin would remove any reason for living a holy life.

reply.text: The objection treats sin as a commercial debt. A creditor must accept his money from anyone, but a judge need not accept a substitute. Boyce, following A. A. Hodge, answers that a penal satisfaction differs from a money payment, and when the sovereign himself appoints the substitute the whole arrangement is grace. Paul holds both halves together in one sentence: sinners are declared righteous as a gift through Christ's redemption, and God set him forth as a sacrifice of atonement, so that he is just and justifies believers (Romans 3:24-26). The gift is free to us because it cost God, not because it cost nothing, and the God who forgives is the one who provides the sacrifice (Romans 8:32). The charge that this breeds careless living Paul raised and answered himself: those who died with Christ cannot go on living in sin (Romans 6:1-4).

heldBy: Socinian writers, as James P. Boyce reports them (1882)
objections.objection: Animal sacrifice belongs to the childhood of religion, to gods who must be fed or bribed. A mature faith should outgrow it. To say God needed blood before he would forgive makes him less moral than a decent human parent, who forgives without demanding that anything die.

reply.text: In Israel blood was never food for God. Leviticus gives the reason in God's own words: a creature's life is in its blood, and God himself gave it on the altar to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11). Sacrifice was his provision, not a bribe offered to him. On the Day of Atonement the blood cleansed the sanctuary from the people's sins (Leviticus 16:15-19), and Hebrews says plainly that the blood of animals could never take sin away (Hebrews 10:4-10); it pointed to a person and a willing obedience, as Boyce traces it. Blood stands for a life given up in death, the wage sin earns (Romans 6:23). Hebrews' point is not that God enjoys death, but that forgiveness costs a life (Hebrews 9:22).

objections.objection: Penal substitution divides the Trinity into an angry Father and a loving Son. It makes violence the means of salvation and sanctifies retribution, so that the cross, instead of ending the cycle of violence, becomes its highest example. Jesus taught his followers not to repay evil, yet this account says God's own justice demands repayment.

reply.text: Scripture does not set the Father's anger against the Son's love. Calvin, often blamed for the doctrine, wrote that God loved us before the reconciliation and was never hostile to his Son, even while the Son bore judgment. The plan is the Father's, and the Son offers himself by the eternal Spirit (Hebrews 9:14): one will, not two. The Servant himself was guilty of no violence (Isaiah 53:9). Lawless men killed Jesus, and yet God's purpose was being done (Isaiah 53:10; Acts 2:23). Judging evil is not cruelty: a God who never judged it would be indifferent to its victims. At the cross God judges sin by bearing it himself, and so shows himself just (Romans 3:25-26).

citations.locator: No. 1910, 'The Heart of the Gospel' (18 July 1886)

objections.objection: For a thousand years the church spoke of the cross as victory over death and the devil, or as a ransom. Anselm introduced satisfaction in 1098, and only the Reformers turned it into the Father punishing the Son. A doctrine the first Christians did not hold cannot be the heart of the gospel.

reply.text: Part of this is true. The early Fathers wrote no treatise on penal substitution; their main themes were victory, ransom and the renewal of humanity, and the developed legal statement belongs to the Reformation. But the substitution itself is early. Athanasius, around 318 (some date it to the 330s), wrote that the Word gave his body to death in place of all, to pay the debt of death that all owed, and that he died on a cross because he came to bear the curse that lay on us (On the Incarnation 8-9, 20, 25). Augustine wrote that Christ underwent death, the penalty of sin, for our sake and without sin of his own, and so could expiate sins (City of God 10.24). Irenaeus spoke of Christ redeeming us with his own blood (Against Heresies 5.1.1). The Reformers sharpened what was already there. For Baptists the deciding question is not a doctrine's age but what Scripture says, and the Fathers read the same texts (Isaiah 53:5-6; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24).

heldBy: Universalists, as Boyce reports them (1882): an atonement made for all must save all
Arminian critics of particular redemption, as Spurgeon (1858) and Boyce report them: if he paid only for some, the offer to all is insincere
objections.objection: Substitution forces a bad choice. If Christ really bore the penalty for every person, God cannot justly punish anyone, so all must be saved. If he bore it only for some, the gospel offered to everyone is offered to many for whom nothing was paid.

reply.text: Baptists answer this in different ways, and the site does not choose between them. Calvinist Baptists, from the London Confessions of 1644 and 1689 to Spurgeon and Boyce, hold particular redemption: Christ died to secure the salvation of those the Father gave him, the sheep for whom the shepherd dies (John 10:11, 15); his death, sufficient for all, is offered to all. General Baptists, in the Orthodox Creed of 1679, and many Southern Baptists today, in the Traditional Statement of 2012, hold that Christ died for every person, pointing to 1 John 2:2 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6; his death, they reply to the first horn, saves only through faith. Andrew Fuller came to stand between them: Christ died for sinners as sinners, general in sufficiency, particular in an application God designed for the elect; and the duty to trust Christ never waits on knowing oneself elect. Boyce judged this mistaken. All affirm the substitution. The Baptist Faith and Message requires personal faith in Christ for salvation and leaves the extent open (article IV).

prompt.text: If the Judge himself bore the sentence, what does that say about how seriously God takes your sin, and how much he loves you? Read Isaiah 53:4-6 again before you answer.

reviews.scope: New objections-and-replies article (step 6), seven pairs. Every cited verse opened in the Berean; Spurgeon, Boyce Lecture XXVIII (1882 printing), Fuller, Athanasius, Anselm, the 1644 confession and the Orthodox Creed read at the cited places by the independent AI review. Findings fixed: the extent of the atonement shown as three Baptist positions (particular, general, Fuller's middle view with Boyce's dissent) without choosing; Berean wording paraphrased; Boyce locators corrected, his line credited to A. A. Hodge as he does; holders described without invented names. Validate clean; depth on target (1,599 words).
